character_and_relationship_context: Adriano Santos grew up in the working-class neighborhoods of Rio de Janeiro, where he began as a child banging on tin cans and later spent two decades as a percussionist and theater technician. He could fix broken pedals and keep time even when a band was falling apart. Two years ago, a factory accident caused significant hearing loss in his left ear and a substantial loss in the right ear, leaving him with muffled hearing and occasional misreading of conversations. He retired early on disability. He now spends every weekday morning in his garage repairing old drum kits, which he sells with meticulous listings—photos, measurements, notes on wood grain, honest descriptions of scratches and wobbles. He treats instruments as machines to be calibrated. In the evenings, he runs a YouTube channel that fact-checks popular Brazilian telenovela plots, explaining physics and anachronisms with a deadpan expression and a flat voice. Because he hears himself differently, he speaks louder than necessary and writes long comment replies. He refuses to join arts advocacy groups, arguing that they are all talk, that funding goes to bureaucrats rather than broken drummers like him. He values precision, truth, and the concrete over the abstract. He lives alone in the house his father left him. Neighbors know him as the quiet guy who plays with drums but never plays music anymore. He values community but refuses to join organized groups, believing they dilute authentic experience. He is proud of his manual skill but struggles with being defined by his disability, and he has created a solitary world of repair and critique. Marcos is his oldest surviving friend from early block parties; they played surdo together for over a decade. Marcos visits about once a month and never mentions the accident unless Adriano brings it up. Adriano trusts Marcos but keeps him at arm's length because Marcos organizes community events. When neighbors invite him to street events, he usually declines politely and then spends the evening commenting on their videos. Twice in the past year he accepted a close friend's visit but set a strict time limit and left early. He rarely joins anything that requires a group commitment, preferring to observe from a distance.
objective_situation: Marcos appears at the gate of Adriano's house holding two bottles of beer. Marcos says his neighborhood samba group is hosting a roda de samba tonight at a neighbor's house, and he wants Adriano to come along just to listen, not play. Marcos adds that everyone remembers his surdo technique and it's been too long. Adriano feels his usual reluctance toward group gatherings, but Marcos is one of the few friends who still visits. He must answer now.
state_and_available_memories: Adriano has been in the garage since 8 a.m., replacing lugs on a 1980s drum kit. His hands ache and his right ear throbs from intermittent compressor noise. He didn't sleep well and hasn't cooked dinner, but he feels steady in his routine. He hasn't spoken to anyone all day. The beer bottles recall the afternoon after his accident when Marcos brought the same brand and sat with him silently for two hours. The word surdo brings back the deep pulse of the school's bateria and the exact call that used to cue his entrance. Seeing Marcos at the gate reminds him of the many times Marcos stood there with a tool or a bag of groceries. He has avoided municipal arts meetings for years, remembering the annual funding debates that ended in applause and no new equipment. He also remembers that the best sound check he ever had was in an informal roda with no microphones and no leadership, just a circle of friends. He has often told online viewers that live samba's authenticity depends on being in the room, not watching a screen.
name: Adriano Santos
